title: How to Secure AI-Generated Code in 6 Steps | Salt Security
summary: Learn how to secure AI-generated code with a practical workflow: secure prompts, automated scanning, dependency checks, targeted review, and governance.
body_markdown:
## Verify Every Dependency Before It Enters Your Codebase


AI coding tools sometimes suggest packages that do not exist. The[USENIX Security 2025 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10279) describes this as a new form of package confusion attack: an attacker registers the hallucinated name on a public registry such as PyPI or npm, publishes malicious code under it, and waits for a developer to run the install command the AI suggested. The researchers found the problem was persistent and systemic across models.


Before installing any package an AI tool suggests, confirm three things:


1. **It is real.** Check that the package exists on the official registry under the exact name, and watch for near-miss spellings of popular libraries.
2. **It is actively maintained.** Look at release history, maintainer activity, and download volume. A brand-new package with no history deserves scrutiny.
3. **It is free of known vulnerabilities.** Run it through your software composition analysis tool before it reaches a lockfile.


Then keep a software bill of materials (SBOM). An SBOM is a list of the open-source and third-party components in your code, with their versions, licenses, and patch status, as the[CMS Information Security and Privacy Program](https://security.cms.gov/learn/software-bill-materials-sbom) explains. Generating it in CI gives you a running record of every component an AI tool has introduced, so you can respond quickly when a new vulnerability is disclosed.


## Reserve Human Review for High-Risk Changes


Automated tools cannot catch every business logic flaw, and reviewers cannot read every AI-generated line at machine speed. Focus human review where a mistake costs the most:


- **Authentication and authorization.** Access control deserves the closest look. Gartner's[How to Secure Custom-Built AI Agents report](https://content.salt.security/GartnerSecureCustomAIAgents_LP.html) finds that access control issues will cause most agentic security failures.
- **Cryptography.** Algorithm choice, key handling, and random number generation.
- **Sensitive data handling.** Anything that touches PII, payment data, or health data, including where that data is logged.
- **New external endpoints, agent tools, and MCP servers.** Each new API or MCP integration expands your attack surface. Gartner also notes that most published MCP servers lack content sanitization, making public MCP servers a significant and underestimated attack vector.


Separate the person who prompted a risky change from the person who approves it. A developer who iterated with an AI assistant until the code worked is the least likely to spot what the assistant got wrong.


Review also does not end at merge. As Salt's Nick Rago explains in[Your AI Transformation Needs Runtime Protection for the Whole Agentic Estate](https://salt.security/blog/your-ai-transformation-needs-runtime-protection-for-the-whole-agentic-estate) , a single prompt can travel from an agent through an LLM and MCP servers to the APIs that run your business. An attacker who learns about an exposed tool can skip the agent entirely and call the API behind it. The code your AI assistants write becomes part of that path, so validate it at runtime as well as in review.


## Set a Lightweight Governance Policy for AI Coding Tools


Write a short, practical policy rather than a lengthy compliance document. A policy people can read in five minutes is a policy people follow.[Salt Code](https://salt.security/code) names the alternative plainly: when policies live in PDFs, wikis, and tribal knowledge, the AI building your software has read none of them.


At minimum, the policy should state:


- **Where AI tools are allowed.** Which assistants are approved, for which repositories, and whether any code (such as cryptographic or payment modules) is off-limits.
- **What must be scanned.** The SAST, SCA, and secrets checks every AI-assisted change must pass, and where they run.
- **What needs human review.** The high-risk categories from the previous section.
- **Who owns exceptions.** A named owner who can approve a deviation and record why.


Tag AI-generated commits so teams can trace an issue back to how the code was created. Commit metadata is what made GitGuardian's Claude Code findings possible in the first place: the researchers could compare leak rates only because those commits carried a co-author tag. The same tagging lets your team measure whether its AI-assisted code is getting safer over time.


## Automate Enforcement With an AI Code Governance Platform


Every step above works only if developers remember to do it, on every prompt, under deadline pressure. A dedicated governance platform applies these steps automatically. When evaluating one, look for:


- **Prevention at the point of generation.** Policies should shape the code while the AI writes it, not only flag problems after commit.
- **Coverage across your assistants.** Developers use several tools; one policy model should govern them all.
- **Pipeline and runtime enforcement.** Checks in CI/CD that block violations before production, plus monitoring of how APIs, MCP servers, and agents actually behave once deployed.
- **Prioritization based on real exposure.** Findings ranked by what is reachable and exploitable, so teams fix what matters first.
- **Clear audit trails.** Records of which policies applied to which code, for compliance and incident response.


[Salt Code](https://salt.security/code) is built for this workflow. Its goal is to make AI-generated code compliant as soon as it is created, not after the fact. Salt Code connects the Salt Posture Governance Engine to the tools developers already use and carries enforcement from prompt to production:


1. **Discover** every API, MCP server, and AI agent integration across code repositories and cloud environments.

3. **Govern in the pipeline** by validating policy in CI/CD and pull requests and blocking violations before production.
4. **Validate at runtime** by monitoring APIs, MCP integrations, and agents for policy violations, posture gaps, and anomalous activity.
5. **Remediate and improve** by feeding runtime findings back into developer workflows and the AI assistants themselves.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### How do you prompt AI to write more secure code?


State security requirements in the prompt rather than asking only for the feature. Ask explicitly for input validation, parameterized queries, authentication and authorization checks, safe handling of tokens and IDs, and no hardcoded secrets. Keep a shared library of vetted prompts so the whole team starts from the same baseline, and use a tool that injects security policies automatically so protection does not depend on memory.


### Do you still need human review of AI-generated code?


Yes, but targeted. Veracode found that even the best-performing model in its 2026 testing still failed about one in three security tasks. Focus human review on authentication and authorization, cryptography, sensitive data handling, and new endpoints, agent tools, or MCP servers, and let automation handle the rest.


### Which tools help secure AI-generated code?


A layered set: static analysis (SAST) for insecure patterns, software composition analysis (SCA) for vulnerable or nonexistent packages, secrets detection before commit, SBOM generation for component tracking, and an AI code governance platform such as Salt Code that enforces policy inside the coding assistant itself.


### How do you keep secrets out of AI-generated code?


Never paste real credentials into prompts or example code. Reference secrets from a vault or secrets manager, run secrets detection in the IDE and as a pre-commit and CI check, and audit MCP configuration files, which GitGuardian found to be a growing source of leaked credentials. If a secret does leak, rotate it immediately rather than only deleting it from the latest commit.


### Should AI-generated code go through a separate review process from human-written code?


It should meet the same security bar, with extra checks matched to how AI fails: package verification, secrets scanning, and closer review of high-risk categories. Tagging AI-assisted commits makes this practical, because it lets you route those changes to the right checks and measure results over time.
